quests.explanation: Dropping the final 'e' before adding '-ation' is the same standard pattern seen throughout this level.
From Latin 'vigilare' (to watch), an invigilator is the person who 'watches over' students during an exam.

quests.hint: It's related to 'plagiarism' — verb form: PLA-GIA-RIZE.
quests.explanation: Sharing a root with 'plagiarism,' this verb describes the act of presenting someone else's work as your own.
This compound word describes 'work' assigned as part of a 'course' of study, distinct from final exams.

quests.hint: Short word, tricky plural: THESIS becomes THESES.
quests.explanation: Borrowed from Greek, 'thesis' has an irregular plural 'theses' rather than the expected 'thesises' — worth memorizing both forms.
From Greek 'biblion' (book) and 'graphein' (to write), a bibliography is literally a list of 'books written' or referenced.
This compound word describes a 'note' placed at the 'foot' (bottom) of a page for extra information.

quests.hint: Remember the irregular plural: APPENDIX becomes APPENDICES.
quests.explanation: Like many words from Latin, 'appendix' has an irregular plural form, 'appendices,' alongside the more modern 'appendixes.'

quests.hint: Short and simple: T-Y-P-O, just four letters.
quests.explanation: This informal shortened word for 'typographical error' is spelled exactly as it sounds, making it easy to remember.
This slightly formal word for 'late' is often used in school settings to describe arriving after the scheduled time.
Combining 'neighbor' with the suffix '-hood' (a state or area) describes the surrounding area where neighbors live.
A common mistake is using only one 'r'; 'errand' needs both, similar to other doubled-consonant words like 'arrive.'
The prefix 'ap-' (a form of 'ad-') often doubles its consonant before a root starting with the same letter, as in 'appoint' and 'apply.'

quests.hint: Short word: C-H-O-R-E, with a silent 'e.'
quests.explanation: Despite being only five letters, 'chore' has a silent final 'e' that changes the 'o' to a long sound.
Borrowed from French, 'routine' has just one 't,' a spot where learners sometimes mistakenly double the letter.
From Latin 'commutare' (to change completely), 'commute' originally meant to exchange, evolving to mean a regular trip to work.

quests.hint: Remember the 'au' makes an 'aw' sound: LAUN-DRY.
quests.explanation: Borrowed from French 'lavanderie' (a place for washing), 'laundry' keeps an unusual vowel combination worth memorizing by sight.
This compound word simply joins 'dish' and 'washer,' describing the appliance that washes your dishes.
From Greek 'therme' (heat) and 'statos' (standing), a thermostat keeps temperature 'standing' steady.
From French 'mort' (dead) and 'gage' (pledge), a mortgage was historically a 'dead pledge' — the silent 't' is a tricky leftover from this origin.
This compound word literally describes the 'lord' (owner) of the 'land' or property being rented.

quests.hint: It's 'ten' plus 'ant' — unrelated to the number ten: TEN-ANT.
quests.explanation: From Latin 'tenere' (to hold), a tenant is someone who 'holds' or occupies a rented property.
From Latin 'utilis' (useful), 'utility' describes a useful service like water, gas, or electricity provided to a home.
Dropping the final 'e' before adding '-ance' is the same familiar pattern as 'resemble' to 'resemblance.'
From Latin 'praemium' (reward), a premium now describes either a regular insurance payment or a higher-quality product.
The suffix '-ible' means 'able to be,' so a deductible amount is the part of a cost 'able to be' subtracted before insurance pays.
This straightforward compound word describes a 'list' of items to 'check' off one by one.
This compound word describes a journey that goes 'round' (out and back), unlike a one-way trip.
From Latin 'terminus' (boundary or end), an airport terminal is the building marking the 'end' point of your journey on the ground.
This informal compound word describes a short trip to 'get away' from your usual routine.
